(i) indirect standardization is a valid method of profiling, and (ii) the performance of indirect standardization is robust to the presence of omitted variables.

(i) the indirect standardization approach to institutional profiling is a valid method of quality assessment in multilevel settings, (ii) the standardization method is robust in terms of its performance in null and nonnull settings, (iii) the standardization approach is robust in the sense that it is not sensitive to the inadvertent or deliberate omission of adjustment variables, (iv) the random-effects reformulation of the indirect standardization method is a valid alternative to the fixed-effects approach, (v

the indirect standardization method is a viable alternative to hierarchical modelling for creating performance indicators when the response variable of interest is dichotomous and when the institutional outputs are not nested within a larger hierarchy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods for measuring the quality of institutions, such as hospitals and schools.
the creation of performance measures in multilevel settings.
the development of statistical methods to measure quality in the higher education sector, and more broadly, in other multilevel settings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the profiling methods that we study are useful in settings in which there are a large number of institutions, the outcome is dichotomous and there are no other variables of interest that are measured at the level of the individual unit.
the profiling method is not a good way to assess the quality of universities in the UK.

the profiling method is a useful and valid approach for the indirect measurement of the quality of institutions, but that it is important to be aware of the limitations of the method and of the potential for bias in its application.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the standardization method is a simple, powerful and flexible tool for quality assessment in multilevel settings with a binary outcome.

, in the context of the UK higher education setting, we have found a way of measuring quality which is simple to use, easy to understand, has a sound statistical basis, is robust to the inadvertent inclusion of irrelevant variables and can be used in a longitudinal framework.

the indirect standardization method, which is easy to implement, has the potential for large sample equivalence to the fixed effects hierarchical modelling approach, but is sensitive to omitted covariates and may be less powerful than fixed effects hierarchical modelling when the number of clusters is relatively small.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the standardization approach can be a powerful and useful method for the creation of performance measures in multilevel settings.
indirect standardization can be a useful and robust approach to the indirect measurement of the quality of processes unfolding in hierarchical or multilevel settings.
indirect standardization, a method that has been in use for over 50 years, performs surprisingly well in the context of hierarchical or clustered data, even when the number of clusters is small.
